intro: Mencius and Zhuangzi lived at about the same time, in the fourth century BCE, during the Warring States period. They never mention each other. Their books could hardly be more different. Mencius argues with kings. Zhuangzi tells stories about butchers, frogs, fish and dreams.

In this unit you read both up close. From the Mencius, in James Legge's 1895 translation, you read the child at the well, the king and the ox, the debate with Gaozi and the ranking of the people above the ruler. From the Zhuangzi, in paraphrase, you read Cook Ding, the frog in the well, the fish on the Hao bridge, the butterfly dream and the drum at a funeral.

By the end you will be able to cite the Mencius by book, part and chapter, and the Zhuangzi by chapter. You will explain terms such as the four sprouts, the Mandate of Heaven, perspectivism and the transformation of things, and describe how readers have taken each text.
bigQuestion: How do Mencius's arguments and Zhuangzi's stories each try to change the way a reader sees people and the world?

test.q: In which passage does Mencius describe the child about to fall into a well?
test.why: Mencius 2A.6 gives the child at the well.

test.q: What does Mencius say King Xuan's pity for the ox shows?
choices: He has the feeling needed to rule kindly
test.why: Mencius says the feeling is enough if the king extends it.
The people are the most important element in a nation.

test.q: Who debated Mencius with the willow and water analogies?
Which thinker said human nature is bad?
test.why: Xunzi argued against Mencius in his chapter 23.

test.q: How many virtues grow from the four sprouts?
choices: Four: ren, yi, li and zhi
test.why: Mencius 2A.6 names four beginnings for four virtues.

test.q: In Zhuangzi 3, what does Lord Wenhui learn from Cook Ding?
test.why: The lord says he has learned to nourish life.

test.q: Which chapter holds the frog in the well and the Hao bridge?
test.why: Both stories are in chapter 17, "Autumn Floods."

test.q: What does Zhuangzi dream at the end of chapter 2?

test.why: Guo Xiang edited it to 33 chapters around 300 CE.

test.q: In chapter 18, what does Zhuangzi compare his wife's death to?
test.why: He likens it to the round of the four seasons.

test.q: What does the Ox Mountain analogy say about people who seem to lack goodness?
choices: Their goodness may have been cut back
test.why: Mencius 6A.8 says the bare mountain once had trees.

test.q: Why should writers be careful citing the outer chapters as "Zhuangzi's view"?
choices: Many scholars think followers wrote them
test.why: Authorship of the outer chapters is debated.

test.q: How do Mencius and Zhuangzi differ in method?
choices: Mencius argues to persuade; Zhuangzi tells open-ended stories
Zhuangzi argues with kings; Mencius tells fables only
test.why: Mencius debates; Zhuangzi uses parables and humor.

test.q: Which translation is quoted exactly for the Mencius in this unit?

write.prompt: Mencius and Zhuangzi both use images to change how readers see the world. Cite two or three passages (for example Mencius 2A.6 in Legge's 1895 translation and Zhuangzi chs. 3 and 17 in paraphrase), explain what each says, and describe how readers have understood them.
tips: Cite the Mencius by book, part and chapter and name Legge's 1895 edition.
Say "paraphrased" for the Zhuangzi and name the chapter.
Attribute every view: "Mencius argues," "Guo Xiang read," "some scholars think."
Compare the two thinkers without ranking them.
